**Key Risks — Litigation & Environmental Liabilities (3M)**

1. **Combat Arms Earplugs litigation (Aearo Chapter 11).** 3M committed approximately $1.0 billion (later increased with an additional $0.2 billion for case expenses) to fund the Aearo entities' Chapter 11 process, reflected as a contingent liability on 3M's consolidated balance sheet [E1][E8]. 3M states explicitly that "no liability has been recorded for the Combat Arms Earplugs litigation because the company believes any such liability is not probable and reasonably estimable and the company is not able to estimate a possible loss or range of possible loss at this time" [E1][E5]. The bankruptcy court dismissed the Aearo bankruptcy filings in June 2023, lifting the litigation stay and triggering reconsolidation of Aearo onto 3M's balance sheet with an "immaterial" income-statement impact [E4]. As of Q2 2023, roughly 90,700 unfiled claims sit on an MDL administrative docket and thousands of bellwether-related cases remain, with at least one jury verdict of $5M compensatory/$72M punitive damages against 3M prior to the bankruptcy filing [E5]. This is the single largest, most actively litigated liability in the filings and directly affects Safety and Industrial segment special items and Corporate/unallocated charges [E3].

2. **PFAS/AFFF environmental litigation.** 3M manufactured AFFF containing PFAS for firefighting use from ~1963–2002; as of June 30, 2023 approximately 4,996 lawsuits (including ~46 putative class actions and 451 public water system cases) were pending, mostly consolidated in an MDL in South Carolina [E7]. Multiple state attorneys general (e.g., Maryland, filing two suits in May 2023) have brought or are preparing PFAS contamination claims against 3M, and 3M discloses it is in settlement discussions with several states [E7]. Net costs for PFAS-related matters are tracked as corporate special items [E3].

3. **Respirator mask/asbestos litigation.** Treated alongside Combat Arms and PFAS as one of 3M's three categories of "significant litigation" tracked as special items, with net costs including accrued liability changes, legal fees, and insurance recoveries [E3].

4. **Adequacy of reserves — NOT GROUNDED.** The filings disclose accrual amounts, funding commitments, and case volumes, but 3M does not state — and the retrieved passages do not support — a conclusion that recorded reserves and the $1.0–1.2B funding commitment are *adequate* to cover ultimate exposure. To the contrary, 3M's own language ("not probable and reasonably estimable," "not able to estimate a possible loss or range of possible loss") signals the company itself declines to size the exposure [E1][E5]. Any adequacy determination would require independent actuarial or legal analysis outside this corpus.

**Materiality assessment:** Combat Arms Earplugs and PFAS/AFFF litigation are treated by 3M as material — both are quantified (funding commitments, case counts, charge amounts) and discussed in MD&A as recurring special items [E1][E3][E7][E8], unlike generic boilerplate risk factors. Respirator mask/asbestos litigation is disclosed in the same special-items framework but with less quantification in the retrieved passages and appears secondary in scale.</draft>

company.description: Restrict to one company as named in the corpus.

doc_type.description: Document type as stored in this corpus. Spelling variants such as '10-K' are accepted.

tools.description: Look up exact XBRL facts from SEC companyfacts for one company. Prefer this over text search for any specific financial figure -- the values are exact and carry the form and filing date as provenance.
